title: Find your local Muslim community
whyMatters: Islam was never meant to be practiced alone. The Muslim community (ummah) works something like a family: people celebrate with you, stay with you through the hard parts, and help you keep growing. Finding your local community is one of the most useful things you can do as a new Muslim. One friend or mentor who has been where you are can be the difference between feeling lost and feeling at home.

exactActions.text: Look for a programme for new Muslims
subSteps: Many masjids and centres run something for converts, such as a weekly beginners' class or a convert support group.

Some Canadian masjids run named programmes for converts, such as Convert Care at Islam Care Centre in Ottawa or Convert Connect at MAC Masjid Toronto. The community topic lists more across Canada. Confirm times before you go.
Ask at your masjid, or phone one near you, and ask what they run for new Muslims.

exactActions.text: Introduce yourself to the imam or community leader
subSteps: The imam leads the prayer and is often the person people go to for guidance. Most are glad to meet a new Muslim.
Tell them you recently took your Shahada.
Ask about programs, classes, or study circles for new Muslims.
Ask your questions. Imams expect them and would rather you asked.

exactActions.text: Find a mentor or a study buddy
subSteps: Ask the imam or people at the masjid whether someone could mentor you.
A mentor answers your day-to-day questions, prays with you, and keeps you going.
Look for someone patient who knows their material and will not judge you.
A friend who is also still learning makes a good study partner too.
If local options are thin, online convert groups can fill some of the gap.

exactActions.text: Go to one class or one event
subSteps: Many masjids run weekly halaqas (study circles), potlucks, or social nights.
These are the easiest places to meet people and learn without pressure.
Bring a dish to a potluck. It gives you something to talk about.
If big gatherings are too much, start with a small class or a one-on-one meeting.

timeEstimate: An hour or two a week, building over time

obstacles.problem: I feel like I don't fit in
obstacles.solution: Islam spans more cultures than almost any other religion. Muslims in Canada come from dozens of countries. You belong here as much as the person standing next to you. It can take a few visits before it feels ordinary. Give yourself room and keep turning up, because that is how connection actually builds.

obstacles.problem: I don't have any Muslim friends
obstacles.solution: That is what this step is for. Every Muslim friend you will ever have starts out as a stranger. Masjid events, new Muslim classes, and online groups are all places to start. Be open and give it time. Even one solid connection changes how all of this feels. A local WhatsApp or Telegram group for Muslims in your area is worth joining too.

Islam is practiced across many cultures, and cultural habits often get mixed in with religious ones. It is fine to ask whether something is part of Islam or part of somebody's culture. Hold on to the core teachings first. In time you will enjoy the cultural variety and still be able to tell the two apart.

tinyVersion: If a masjid is too much right now, start with one Muslim, online or in person. A single friend who has your back changes a lot.
unlocksNext: With people around you, you are ready to start reading the Quran and spend time with Allah's own words.
